all_historical_figures.name: Agastya
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Sakalādhikāra', a standard text on consecration followed in South India.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhṛgu
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Kriyādhikāra', a Vaiṣṇava Āgama text quoted for its explanation of consecration.

all_historical_figures.name: Marichi
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as the author of the Vimānārcanā-kalpa, a Vaikhānasā text that provides rules for dividing the sanctum floor-space.

all_historical_figures.name: Viśvakarmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Invoked and worshipped during the consecration rituals as the presiding deity of architecture, sculpture, and the temple structure itself.

all_historical_figures.name: Ācārya / Guru / Sthāpaka
all_historical_figures.significance: The main officiant responsible for conducting the entire consecration ceremony according to scriptural rules.

all_historical_figures.name: Ṛtviks
all_historical_figures.significance: Priests who assist the Ācārya, particularly in the fire rituals (homa).

all_historical_figures.name: Yajamāna
all_historical_figures.significance: The person who has sponsored the project and participates in key rituals.

all_historical_figures.name: Sculptor (Śilpi)
all_historical_figures.significance: Creates the icon and performs the initial preliminary consecration. Formally dismissed after the 'netronmilana' in some traditions.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the region where Agastya's 'Sakalādhikāra' is a standard text for consecration rituals.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Indicates a regional textual tradition for the practices described.

complete_terminology_index.context: A term for consecration, literally meaning providing a firm foundation. Sometimes distinguished from pratiṣṭhā.
A key term for consecration, literally meaning providing a fixed basis. Derived from the invocation 'Om prati-tiṣṭha parameśvara'.

complete_terminology_index.translation: That which has come down; scripture
complete_terminology_index.context: A collection of scriptures that are the primary source for temple construction and consecration rituals.
Describes the transcendent, formless nature of the deity before it is invoked into a form (sakala).
The ultimate knowledge or gnosis that is the pathway to salvation.
In Śaivāgama, represents the principle of pure consciousness.
In Śaivāgama, represents the principle of primordial action or energy.
The aniconic symbol of Śiva, representing pure consciousness.
The base or pedestal of the liṅga, representing Śakti. Also called pīṭha.
The pedestal of the liṅga, representing Śakti. Also called piṇḍikā.
An icon that has been consecrated and is now fit for all worship rituals.
The sequence of immersing an icon in water, milk, grains, etc., as part of the consecration process.
An expression describing the entire process of temple creation, from the first ritual on the soil to the final installation of the idol.
Refers to the temple site and its architectural disposition.
The personification of the building site, conceived as a divine or demonic being, who must be propitiated.
A sacred geometric diagram, here referring to the square grid plan of the temple site.
The ceremony of laying the first bricks of the foundation.
The chief architect-builder of the temple, identified with Brahmā.
The patron who sponsors the construction of the temple, identified with Viṣṇu.
The officiating priest who performs the consecration, identified with Śiva.
A term for a temple, etymologically derived from that which 'pleases the mind'.
A term for a temple, etymologically derived from being built with 'various measurements'.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Traditional doctrine or precept, a collection of sacred scriptures.
complete_terminology_index.context: The primary textual sources for temple construction and consecration rituals.
The foundation layer of the temple, which must be well laid before the sanctum is raised.
A solitary main deity sculpted in stone and fixed to the ground in the sanctum.
A metallic icon used for regular and daily worship, often placed alongside the dhruvārcā.
The central cell or zone of the sanctum floor-space, considered the most sacred spot.
The zone surrounding the Brahma-sthāna, designated for divine beings or the main icon in some traditions.
The zone surrounding the daivika-bhāga.
The outermost zone, considered unsuitable for the installation of primary deities.
Describing the posture of an icon lying down.
Describing the posture of a seated icon.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Arrangement of the plots of the inner sanctum.
complete_terminology_index.context: The title of a section in the Vimānārcanā-kalpa of Marichi.
An aniconic representation of Śiva, prescribed for installation in the Brahma-bhāga in Śaiva shrines.
The foundation-slab for the installation of the main deity.
An immoveable icon, which the Nāradīya-saṁhitā prescribes must be in the Brahma-sthāna.
The individual cells that make up a site plan or maṇḍala.
A diagrammatic plan of a site, such as the 81-cell plan from Bṛhat-saṁhitā.
A temporary or permanent structure erected for rituals.
A raised platform constructed in the center of a maṇṭapa.
A pedestal built on the vedi for placing offerings or the icon.
Metal or wooden pegs driven into the ground at the corners of the ritual area.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Cosmic Man or spirit of the site.
complete_terminology_index.context: A deity personifying the site, who must be propitiated during construction and consecration.
The ritual of infusing an icon or deity representation with life.
The entire installation ceremony is regarded as a yajña.
A guardian spirit of the area who is worshipped during consecration.
A group of sixteen goddesses worshipped during the rituals.
The nine celestial bodies of Hindu astrology, who are propitiated.
A sacrificial altar for fire rituals (homa), which can have various shapes.
Sacred pots filled with water, herbs, and gems, representing deities.
Sacrificial rites involving offerings into a consecrated fire.
Offerings of food made to various deities, especially guardians.
Deities presiding over the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The most important sacred water-pot, representing Sadāśiva.
A pot placed to the left of the Śiva-kumbha, representing the goddess Manonmanī.
A group of five precious stones (gold, diamond, sapphire, ruby, pearl) placed in sacred water-pots.
A mixture of five ingredients (milk, curds, ghee, honey, sugar) used in worship.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Tamil term for temple, referring to the superstructure (vimāna) over the sanctum
complete_terminology_index.context: Defining the sanctum as divine in character.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The superstructure or tower over the sanctum
complete_terminology_index.context: Used interchangeably with 'kōil'.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The central area of the shrine-complex
complete_terminology_index.context: The prescribed location for the main deity.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The midmost square within the sanctum
complete_terminology_index.context: An alternative term for the ideal location of the main deity.
The technical term for the overall ceremony.
Used in rituals to hold sanctified water and other items.
Performed by pouring water from consecrated pots accompanied by Vedic hymns.
Placed in the eight directions for spirits.
The final step in the preliminary consecration.
Selected to lead the consecration ceremony.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Installer; another term for the chief priest
complete_terminology_index.context: Highlights the priest's role in establishing the deity.
Assisting the main ācārya.
A temporary structure built for conducting the homa rituals.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Fire ritual for destroying demonic/negative influences
complete_terminology_index.context: Performed for the pacification of spirits and purification of the area.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Fire ritual related to Vāstu, the science of architecture
complete_terminology_index.context: A preliminary rite before the main consecration.
Used to decorate the yāga-śālā.
Ritual to cleanse the icon of impurities from the sculpting process.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The five products of the cow (milk, curds, ghee, urine, dung)
complete_terminology_index.context: Used for purification baths.
A key ritual to bestow sight upon the icon.
Synonym for netronmīlana.
A major purificatory ritual for the icon.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A golden stylus covered with a cotton wick
complete_terminology_index.context: The instrument used for the 'opening of the eyes' ceremony.
Used to screen the icon during the 'netronmīlana' ritual.
A series of rituals for purification by immersing the icon in various substances.
A preliminary ritual to ritually heal the scars on the icon from sculpting.
A purificatory ritual performed after jalādhivāsa.
A ritual of placing divine energies, mantras, or cosmic principles onto the body of the icon.
The sequence of infusing vital power into the icon.
The final adhivāsa where the icon is laid to rest for the night.
A ceremonial pot of water placed at the head of the icon's bed during śayyādhivāsa.
One of the prescribed adhivāsas.
The ritual of infusing vitality into the icon.
Consecration ceremony for the entire temple structure.
The foundation slab placed in the pit under the icon.
The slab placed above the kūrma-śilā.
A ritual adhesive made of eight ingredients used to fix the icon to its base.
The pedestal on which the icon is finally installed.
The predetermined time for the installation ceremony.
The act of fixing the icon to its pedestal.
Ceremonial waving of camphor light before the icon.
A ritual following the final installation.
